summary: This unit teaches you to lead and support staff who work away from the main office: field staff, home-based staff, lone workers and people on a hybrid pattern. You will learn to set expectations and measure results fairly, choose communication channels, run online meetings and one-to-ones, protect health, safety, wellbeing and information, build trust and team spirit, work out the costs, and review whether the arrangement is working.

blocks.p: This unit is for supervisors and managers in Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies who lead people they do not see every day. **Offsite staff** are employees who do their work mainly away from the main workplace: sales representatives on the road, carers visiting clients, technicians at customers' premises, security officers at client sites, and office workers who work from home.

Leading offsite staff uses the same skills as leading any team: clear goals, good communication, fair treatment and care for people. What changes is that you cannot rely on seeing people at their desks. You must replace **watching** with **agreed results, regular contact and trust**, and you must plan carefully for safety, security and costs.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Set up the arrangement
Agree a written offsite work policy and individual arrangements: who may work offsite, where, when, with what equipment.
Set expectations and manage performance
Agree goals, standards, contact hours and response times; measure results fairly; give feedback and recognition.
Communicate and coordinate
Choose the right channel for each purpose, keep staff informed, share schedules and files, and cope with weak signal and time differences.
Facilitate online meetings and one-to-ones
Prepare, run and follow up a team meeting online; hold private, supportive one-to-ones.
Protect health, safety and wellbeing
Manage lone working, road travel, home workstations, stress and isolation; use check-in and escalation steps.
Protect information
Set and enforce simple security rules for devices, files, passwords and customer data.
Build trust, team spirit and fairness
Include offsite staff in decisions, induction and development; deal with conflict early.
Control costs and review
Work out allowances, mileage and savings correctly; review output, service, costs and staff views.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions and some short calculations (percentages, allowances, mileage, savings).
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms such as lone worker, VPN, escalation, asynchronous) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practical tasks**: planning the leadership arrangements for an offsite team, and running an online meeting and a remote one-to-one, with written records.

blocks.note: Work every calculation twice. In the exam, one wrong digit or a forgotten ×12 for a yearly figure is the most common way to lose marks.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Offsite work: types, benefits, risks and policy

blocks.p: Offsite working is not one thing. The right way to lead people depends on the type of offsite work they do.

head: Type
Description
Main leadership concern
rows: Home-based (remote)
Works from home most or all of the time, for example data entry, accounts, writing, customer support.
Isolation, workstation, hours, security of data at home.
Field-based
Spends the day travelling between customers or sites, for example sales representatives, inspectors, technicians.
Road safety, scheduling, reaching the company system in areas of weak signal.
Lone worker
Works alone without close or direct supervision, for example a carer, a security officer at a remote post, a meter reader.
Personal safety, check-ins, escalation when contact is lost.
Hybrid
Splits time between the office and another place.
Fairness between office and offsite staff; planning which days people are in.
Cross-border or time-zone
Works from another country or at different hours, for example staff serving overseas clients.
Meeting times, legal and tax questions (take advice), fairness.

head: Benefits
Risks
rows: Saves office space and travel time
Wider choice of staff and flexible hours
Can raise output and staff satisfaction
Keeps the business running when the office cannot be used, for example after a hurricane or flood
Isolation and loss of team spirit
Poor communication and misunderstandings
Safety risks that nobody sees
Weak information security
Unfair treatment of people who are seen less often
Overwork, because it is hard to switch off

blocks.p: Good leadership keeps the benefits and controls the risks. This is why the arrangement should be planned, written down and reviewed.
A **written offsite work policy** (also called a remote work policy) tells everyone what is expected. It protects both the firm and the employee. A good policy covers:

ul: Who is eligible, and how a request is made and approved.
Working hours, core contact hours and response times.
Where work may be done, and any places that are not allowed (for example public places for confidential work).
Equipment and allowances: what the employer provides, who maintains it and what is claimed back.
Health and safety duties, including workstation checks and lone worker rules.
Information security rules.
How performance will be measured and reviewed.
How the arrangement can be reviewed, changed or ended, with notice.

blocks.p: Each person then agrees an **individual arrangement** in writing: their days, hours, place of work, equipment and contact times. Terms that change the employment contract should follow employment law and be agreed with the employee, not simply announced.

blocks.note: Offsite staff are still employees. The employer's duty of care and its duties under the occupational safety and health law do not stop at the office door. Pay, leave, discipline and fair treatment follow the employment law and the firm's normal policies.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The most important change when you lead offsite staff is to manage by **results**, not by presence. You cannot see how long someone sits at a desk, and counting hours online or camera time is a poor measure of work. Agree what good work looks like, then check that it is delivered.

blocks.h: What to agree at the start

ul: **Goals and targets**: what the person must achieve, for example visits made, cases closed, orders taken, reports finished.
**Standards**: how well the work must be done: accuracy, customer feedback, deadlines.
**Contact hours**: the times when the person can be reached, usually core hours rather than all day.
**Response times**: how quickly messages are answered, for example urgent calls within 15 minutes, emails within one working day.
**Reporting**: what is reported, how often and in what form, for example a short weekly report or an entry in the shared job system.
**The meeting rhythm**: for example a short daily check-in, a weekly team call and a monthly one-to-one.

blocks.note: Write the expectations down in a one-page **team charter** or in each person's arrangement. Expectations that are only spoken are forgotten or remembered differently.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Measure
Fair?
Why
rows: Work completed against an agreed target
Yes
It measures the result the business needs.
Quality: errors, complaints, customer scores
Yes
It shows whether the work is done well, not only how much.
Meeting deadlines and response times
Yes
They can be checked and were agreed in advance.
Hours logged online or time the camera is on
Poor
It measures presence, not output. It also invites people to look busy.
Messages sent late at night
Poor
It rewards overwork and punishes people who keep proper hours.
Constant phone calls to check on the person
Poor
It signals distrust and interrupts the work.

blocks.p: To find the **percentage of a target reached**, divide the result by the target and multiply by 100.
Worked example: a field representative must make 80 client visits in a month and makes 68. Percentage = 68 ÷ 80 × 100 = **85%**. Check: 85% of 80 = 0.85 × 80 = 68.
A second example: lone workers must make 60 safety check-ins in a week and make 57. 57 ÷ 60 × 100 = **95%**. Check: 0.95 × 60 = 57.

Offsite staff should record their work in an agreed system, such as a shared job schedule, a case system or a simple weekly log. The purpose is to check pay, workload and progress **fairly**, and to let others see who is where. It is not to watch every minute. Records also protect staff: they show when someone is overloaded.

Some tools can track phone locations, screens or keystrokes. Before using any, ask whether it is necessary, whether it is proportionate, and whether staff have been told. The data protection law is about collecting only what you need, for a clear purpose, and keeping it secure. Tracking staff outside working hours, or tracking family members, is not acceptable. Clear results and good records are fairer and build more trust than secret monitoring.

flow: Notice the trend (for example two months in a row)
Talk privately to the person to find the cause
Check for causes you control: workload, tools, unclear targets, safety, wellbeing
Agree support and a short plan with dates
Review progress at an agreed time
Use the formal procedure only if the problem continues after support

blocks.p: Starting with discipline, a pay cut or secret observation damages trust and ignores the real cause. Talk first.
With offsite staff, communication does not happen by chance in the corridor. You must plan it. A good **communication plan** says which channel is used for what, how often, and who leads it.

head: Feature
Live (synchronous)
Delayed (asynchronous)
rows: Examples
Phone call, video call, in-person meeting
Email, shared documents, messages read later, recorded updates
Best for
Sensitive or complex matters: feedback, bad news, problem solving, building relationships
Routine updates, instructions, information that needs a record, people in different time zones or shifts
Weakness
Everyone must be free at the same time; too many calls interrupt work; no record unless notes are kept
Tone is easily misread; replies may be slow; questions go unanswered

blocks.p: Match the channel to the message. A contract ending or a change in someone's role should be given by **live video or phone, followed in writing**. A short text to the whole team is wrong for bad news. A routine timetable change can go by message.

blocks.note: After an important phone or video discussion, confirm what was agreed **in writing**. Both sides then have a record to check, and misunderstandings are caught early.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A regular schedule of short check-ins and team calls, not contact only when something has gone wrong.
One place where news, schedules and documents are shared, so offsite staff get information at the same time as office staff.
Time at the start of calls for news and successes, not only tasks.
Reply to staff within the same response times you expect from them.

blocks.p: Leaders set the example. If you expect staff to answer within a day, answer them within a day.

When people work in different places, jobs can be doubled or missed. A **shared live schedule** that everyone can see, a job list with the owner of each job and a clear way to hand work over solve most of these problems. For documents, use **one shared file with version control** so there are not five different copies by email.

ul: Ask first whether the tool is **secure** and suits the work, not which has the most features or the best colours.
Make sure staff are trained to use it, and have a named person to call for help.
Agree what each tool is for: for example chat for quick questions, email for formal records, the job system for tasks.

blocks.p: Parts of rural Jamaica have weak mobile signal. A good plan includes **offline ways of working** (forms or notes that can be uploaded later), a back-up way to reach the office such as a voice call, and a named support contact. It does not stop work when the signal is poor, and it does not tell staff to buy their own solutions.
When staff work in another country or time zone, agree meeting times that suit both places, rotate inconvenient times fairly, and record meetings or notes for people who cannot attend.

sections.title: Facilitating online meetings and remote one-to-ones

blocks.p: An online meeting needs more planning than a meeting in a room, because it is harder to read faces, easy to talk over each other and easy for quiet people to disappear. To **facilitate** is to guide the meeting so that it reaches its purpose and everybody takes part.

flow: Decide the purpose and who needs to attend
Send an agenda, key information and questions to think about in advance
Choose a time that suits everyone and check the tool and connections; offer a phone dial-in
Appoint a note-taker and someone to watch the chat
Open: welcome people, state the purpose, agree ground rules
Run the discussion: invite each person, keep time, summarise
Close: confirm actions with owners and dates
Send the notes and action log within a day

ul: **Ground rules**: one speaker at a time, use the raise-hand tool, cameras on where possible, mute when not speaking, no side conversations.
**Include everyone**: ask each person by name, use a round where everyone speaks, use the chat or a poll for quieter people.
**Keep time**: an agenda with time for each item; park items that are off topic.
**Handle technical problems**: if someone's connection fails, summarise for them, invite them to give their view by chat or phone afterwards.
**Recognise success** at the start, so the meeting is not only problems.

head: Problem in the meeting
What the facilitator does
rows: One person talks too much
Thank them, then ask others by name; use a time limit per person.
Someone stays silent
Ask them directly and kindly, or ask for views in the chat.
Weak connection
Offer phone dial-in, switch off video, summarise what they missed.
Conversation goes off topic
Note it in a parking list and return to the agenda.
No one volunteers for actions
Ask people by name, agree an owner and a date for every action.

blocks.p: A **one-to-one** is a private conversation between you and one member of staff. For offsite staff it is the main way to discover problems early, give feedback and show that they matter. Hold them regularly, for example every two to four weeks, and keep the time even when things are busy.

ul: Choose a private place and a time that suits them. Do not hold it where others can listen in.
Start by asking how they are, not only about the work.
Give feedback **privately**, with specific examples, and listen to their view.
Agree support: workload changes, training, a different schedule.
Agree actions with dates and confirm them in a short written note.
Do not criticise anyone in a group chat or copy their manager into a sharp email.

blocks.note: When a worker's results have slipped and they seem stressed, the first aim is to understand the cause and offer support. A written follow-up should be calm and clear: what was agreed, who does what and when you will review.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The employer's **duty of care** means it must protect the health and safety of staff wherever they work. A manager must assess the risks of offsite work and put controls in place. Different offsite types have different risks.

head: Offsite situation
Main risks
Controls
rows: Home-based
Poor workstation and posture, long hours at a screen, electrical hazards, stress, isolation
Workstation guidance and check, a suitable chair where needed, breaks, agreed hours, regular contact
Field staff on the road
Road accidents, fatigue, robbery, vehicle breakdown, bad weather
Journey planning, rest breaks, no phone use while driving, vehicle checks, safe routes, an emergency contact
Lone workers
Violence, accidents, medical emergency, no one knows there is a problem
Risk assessment of each site or client, check-in system, escalation steps, emergency contacts, training

blocks.p: **Ergonomics** is fitting the workplace to the worker. A good home workstation has a chair that supports the lower back, feet flat on the floor or a footrest, the top of the screen about at eye level, the keyboard and mouse so that the forearms are level, good lighting without glare, and safe electrical connections (no overloaded sockets or trailing cables). Give guidance, have each workstation checked (a photo or video check is often enough), and provide basic equipment where the policy says so.
A check-in system is only useful if someone acts when a check-in is missed. This is called **escalation**: passing the problem to a more senior person or to emergency help when a step fails.

flow: The worker checks in at the agreed times (for example at start, at each site and at finish)
A named person records each check-in
A missed check-in: the named person phones the worker at once
No reply: try again and phone the client or site contact
Still no contact within the agreed time: inform the manager and go to the site or send help
Anything suggesting danger: call the police or emergency services immediately
Record what happened and review the procedure afterwards

blocks.note: A missed check-in is never to be ignored, noted for an appraisal or left until the next shift. Agree the time limits for each step in advance so no one has to guess.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November. For field staff spread across parishes, a **warning plan** says who contacts each person, how, and how often; what staff do (stop work, go to a safe place, report in); and when work resumes. When a warning is issued, contact each person, confirm they are safe and give instructions. Do not wait for them to call in, and do not tell them to finish work as planned.
**Wellbeing** means a person's health, safety and contentment. Because you do not see offsite staff every day, you must watch for signs in other ways.

head: Warning signs
How a manager responds
rows: Missing meetings or replying more slowly
A change of tone in messages
Messages sent very late at night
A drop in quality or output
A cheerful person becoming quiet
Ask privately, by call or video, how they are
Listen without judging
Review the workload and deadlines
Offer support: flexible hours, training, time off, an employee assistance service if the firm has one
Follow up and check again

blocks.p: To reduce isolation use regular team calls, **buddy pairs** (two staff who check in with each other), occasional meet-ups, shared news and recognition. A survey can show the scale: if 9 of 15 home-based staff often feel isolated, that is 9 ÷ 15 × 100 = **60%**, a serious problem to act on, not a feature of the job.

When staff work offsite, company and customer information travels with them. Laptops and phones are stolen from cars and homes, documents are left in public places, family members see screens, public Wi-Fi is insecure and staff use personal email or memory sticks. Scam emails are also harder to check when you cannot ask the person at the next desk.

head: Risk
Control
rows: Lost or stolen device
Passwords or PINs, screen locks, encryption, remote wipe, report loss at once
Unsafe network
Use the company **VPN** (virtual private network) to reach company systems; avoid public Wi-Fi for confidential work
Weak passwords
Strong, unique passwords; a password manager; two-step login (multi-factor authentication)
Personal accounts and memory sticks
Provide secure company access and shared storage; do not email files to personal accounts
Scam and fake emails
Training; a rule to verify unusual requests by phone; report suspicious messages
Others seeing the screen or papers
Private place to work; lock the screen; lock away papers; do not discuss customers where others can hear
Lost data
Regular backups to a secure place

blocks.p: The firm should have a written policy, train staff on it, give them secure tools and check that the rules are followed. If an employee wants to keep client files on a personal laptop, the right answer is to **provide secure company access** under the policy, not to agree because she works faster.

blocks.note: Customer data often includes personal data. The data protection law is about collecting only what you need, using it for a clear purpose, keeping it secure and not sharing it without cause. Protecting it is a legal duty as well as good practice.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: When a staff member leaves, end their access, recover devices and papers, and remind them of their confidentiality duties. A sales manager leaving for a rival should not take the customer list.

sections.title: Building trust, fairness, induction and development

blocks.p: **Trust** grows when people are reliable, open and fair. Heavy checking, such as calling several times a day, has the opposite effect: staff lose initiative and trust. Instead:

ul: Agree clear outcomes, then give people freedom over how they reach them. An experienced field supervisor who asks to plan her own route can be given that freedom with clear outcomes and regular check-ins.
Keep your own promises and meet the response times you expect of others.
Share information openly with everyone, not only those in the office.
Give regular, specific feedback, privately for problems and publicly for success.

blocks.p: Staff who rarely meet need reasons to feel part of one team. Use regular briefings, shared updates, a place to share news, occasional in-person events or training days, and team goals. Telling people by email that they are a team does nothing. Banning contact between staff or moving people constantly without warning damages team spirit.

Office staff may think offsite staff have an easy life; offsite staff may feel left out of decisions. Apply the **same standards** to both groups, share information with both, consult offsite staff before changes (by call or a quick survey) and explain the reasons. Taking sides, ignoring complaints or ending the arrangement for everyone are all poor responses.

A new offsite employee can feel lost quickly. Plan the induction before the first day: equipment and system access ready, then time with the team in person or in planned video sessions, covering the firm's purpose, role, targets, offsite policy, health and safety, check-in procedures and information security. Give a named contact or buddy and a schedule of early check-ins.

Development must not depend on being at the office. Include offsite staff in online training, give them stretch tasks, mentoring and a development discussion, and consider them for promotion. Do not assume they do not want promotion.

ul: **Recognise** good work promptly and share it with the team. Waiting for the annual appraisal, or assuming people know they did well, wastes the motivation.
**Conflict** that starts in a chat group should be moved to a private call with the people involved. Calm it and agree what happens next. Do not join in publicly, delete the group or ignore it.

sections.title: Costs, resources and reviewing the arrangement

blocks.p: Offsite work moves costs around. Some costs go up (equipment, data, allowances, mileage); others go down (office space, desks, utilities). A manager must calculate them correctly and decide who pays for what.

The **employer** normally provides and maintains the equipment an employee needs to work offsite for the firm, as set out in the policy: laptop, phone or phone allowance, secure access, and where appropriate a chair or other workstation items. The policy should say what is provided, what is an allowance and how claims are made.

head: Item
Working
Answer
rows: Monthly data allowance: 9 staff at J$3,500 each
J$31,500 a month
The same allowance for a year
Mileage: 640 km at J$38 per km
Desks given up: 8 at J$28,000 a month each
Net yearly saving if allowances cost J$378,000
One-off equipment: 9 laptops at J$95,000
First-year net saving with that equipment

blocks.note: A yearly figure needs ×12. A one-off cost appears only in the first year. Later years do not repeat it, though equipment will need replacing in time. Check every sum twice, using a different method if you can.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Review an offsite scheme at least once a year, and sooner if problems appear. Look at four things together:

ul: **Output**: are targets met? Compare with before the change.
**Service**: customer feedback and complaints.
**Costs**: savings against new costs, using the calculations above.
**People**: staff views by survey and one-to-one, including wellbeing and isolation.

blocks.p: A scheme with higher output and lower costs but 60% of staff reporting isolation is a **partial success**: keep it, and act on the isolation with team calls, buddy pairs and meet-ups. Do not judge it on the managing director's opinion alone, on how far staff live from the office, or because no one has complained loudly.

ul: I can describe the types of offsite work and their main leadership concerns.
I can say what an offsite work policy and an individual arrangement should contain.
I can agree goals, standards, contact hours and response times, and measure performance by results.
I can work out the percentage of a target reached and check my answer.
I can choose between live and delayed communication for a given message and confirm decisions in writing.
I can prepare, run and follow up an online meeting, including people with weak connections and quiet members.
I can hold a private one-to-one that gives feedback and agrees support.
I can set up a lone worker check-in and escalation procedure.
I can arrange a safe home workstation and watch for signs of stress and isolation.
I can set practical information security rules and explain why privacy matters when monitoring staff.
I can build trust, deal with conflict and treat offsite and office staff fairly.
I can induct and develop offsite staff.
I can calculate allowances, mileage and savings, and review an offsite arrangement using output, service, costs and staff views.

terms: Offsite staff
Employees who work mainly away from the main workplace.
Hybrid
A pattern in which people work partly in the office and partly elsewhere.
Lone worker
A person who works alone without close or direct supervision.
Duty of care
The employer's responsibility to protect the health and safety of staff wherever they work.
Escalation
Passing a problem to a more senior person or to emergency help when a step fails.
Synchronous
Communication in real time, such as a call or video meeting.
Asynchronous
Communication where replies come later, such as email.
Ergonomics
Fitting the workstation and tasks to the worker.
VPN
Virtual private network: a secure connection to company systems over the internet.
Buddy system
Pairing two workers to check in on and support each other.
Facilitate
Guide a meeting so that it reaches its purpose and everyone takes part.
Wellbeing
A person's health, safety and contentment.
Remote work policy
The written rules for staff who work offsite.
Isolation
The feeling of being cut off from colleagues.

c1.title: A Mandeville agricultural supplier's field team
c1.text: Janet Brown manages seven field sales representatives for a feed and fertiliser supplier in Mandeville. They spend most days visiting farms in Manchester, Clarendon and St Elizabeth. Some farms have poor mobile signal. Until now Janet has judged people by how often she sees them in the office. Targets have never been written down. Last month Raymond made 68 farm visits against a target of 80, and his order values fell for the second month in a row.

c2.title: A Kingston accountancy firm goes hybrid
c2.text: A Kingston accountancy firm has 12 staff and will let them work from home three days a week. The managing partner, Mr Leroy Francis, will give each person a data allowance of J$3,500 a month and a laptop costing J$95,000. He expects to give up 4 desks that cost J$28,000 each a month. Some partners worry that office staff will resent those working at home.

c3.title: Meter readers in Westmoreland
c3.text: A water utility contractor in Savanna-la-Mar sends six meter readers alone into rural Westmoreland communities each day. They check in by phone at the start, at midday and at the end of the day. A tropical storm watch has just been announced for the island. Last week one reader missed her midday check-in and her supervisor, busy with paperwork, decided to wait until the afternoon.

c4.title: A Kingston NGO's programme team
c4.text: A Kingston non-governmental organisation has eight programme officers working from home or from community centres in St Thomas, Portland and Trelawny. Its director, Ms Andrea Powell, holds a Monday video meeting. Recently it has run for two hours, she has done most of the talking and two officers rarely speak. One officer, Devon, often has a weak connection. Another, Shanice, has been replying late and her last report had many errors. She told a colleague she is worn out.

c5.title: An Ocho Rios digital marketing agency
c5.text: A small digital marketing agency in Ocho Rios has ten staff who work partly from home. Staff share client files by emailing them to each other and some use personal laptops and memory sticks. One designer has been logging in at midnight to finish work. The owner, Mr Kelvin Rose, is thinking about installing software that records what each person does on screen all day.

questions.q: What should Janet do first to lead her representatives fairly while they are in the field?
o: Require every representative to call her each hour and give their location
Agree written goals, standards, contact hours and reporting with each person
Ask every representative to come to the office on Fridays to be seen working
Fix the exact route and the time of each visit for every representative
questions.why: Fair leadership starts with agreed expectations, written down, so people know what is required and are judged by results. Hourly calls, forced office visits and fixed routes control presence, ignore results and damage trust.

questions.q: Raymond made 68 farm visits against a target of 80. What percentage of the target did he reach?
questions.why: 68 ÷ 80 × 100 = 85%. Check: 85% of 80 = 68. The figure 68% confuses the number of visits with a percentage, and 12% is the shortfall in visits, not the percentage reached.

questions.q: Raymond's order values have fallen for two months in a row. What should Janet do first?
o: Talk privately with him to find the cause and agree support
Reduce his commission for the months in which sales fell
Ask the other representatives to report on how he spends his days
Start the formal disciplinary procedure against him straight away
questions.why: Falling results have causes that may include workload, unclear targets, weak signal or personal problems. Talk first, agree support and review. Pay cuts, secret observation or discipline damage trust and ignore the cause.

questions.q: Some farms have no mobile signal, so representatives cannot reach the order system. What should the plan include?
o: A rule that field visits stop whenever the signal on a farm is weak
A requirement that each representative buys a signal booster at own cost
Offline order forms uploaded later, and a named support contact
Orders taken only at the Mandeville office on weekdays
questions.why: A sound plan lets work continue offline, with a back-up way to reach the office and a support contact. Stopping work or making staff pay for fixes is unfair and costs the business sales.

questions.q: Mr Francis gives each of 12 staff a data allowance of J$3,500 a month. What is the yearly cost?
questions.why: 12 × J$3,500 = J$42,000 a month, and 42,000 × 12 = J$504,000 a year. J$42,000 is only one month. Remember to multiply by 12 for a yearly cost.

questions.q: Giving up 4 desks at J$28,000 each a month, and paying the J$504,000 yearly allowances, what is the net yearly saving?
questions.why: Desks: 4 × 28,000 = 112,000 a month, so 112,000 × 12 = J$1,344,000 a year. Net saving = 1,344,000 − 504,000 = J$840,000. The first year is lower again because of the one-off laptops.

questions.q: What is the result in the first year once the 12 laptops at J$95,000 each are also counted?
o: A net saving of J$840,000
A net saving of J$300,000
A net cost of J$1,140,000
A net cost of J$300,000
questions.why: Laptops: 12 × 95,000 = J$1,140,000, paid once. First-year result = 840,000 − 1,140,000 = −J$300,000, a net cost. In later years the scheme saves J$840,000, before equipment must be replaced.

questions.q: Some partners fear that office staff will resent those who work at home. What is the best approach?
o: Give the office staff extra pay so that they stay content with the change
Use the same standards for both groups and consult everyone
Stop home working for everyone whenever a complaint is received
Tell the office staff the decision is final and not open to discussion
questions.why: Fairness means the same standards, shared information and consultation for everyone, with clear reasons. Compensating, reversing after complaints or shutting down discussion does not deal with the cause of the resentment.

questions.q: A tropical storm watch is announced. What should the contractor's manager do first?
o: Wait for the readers to phone in if they need help during the storm
Post a general notice on the company's social media page
Tell the readers to finish the day's meters before they return to base
Contact every reader, confirm they are safe and give instructions
questions.why: Staff spread over parishes cannot be assumed safe. Contact each person, confirm where they are and tell them what to do under the warning plan. Waiting, posting a general notice or insisting on finishing work leaves lone workers at risk.

questions.q: A reader missed her midday check-in and the supervisor decided to wait until the afternoon. What was wrong with this?
o: The supervisor should have told the reader to send reports by email instead
Escalation should have started at once, as she might be in danger
The reader should have been warned for missing the agreed check-in time
The supervisor should have waited for the end-of-day check-in to be sure
questions.why: A check-in system works only if a missed check-in triggers action straight away: phone the reader, try the client, then escalate to help. Delay can cost a lone worker her safety. The aim is protection, not punishment.

questions.q: Which control best protects the readers who work alone in rural communities?
o: A check-in system with a named person to act on missed calls
A written reminder for readers to be careful on every visit
A rule that readers may work only in the cooler morning hours
A list of the contractor's directors and their phone numbers
questions.why: Controls need a system and a person responsible for it. General advice, shorter hours or a list of numbers do not ensure that anyone notices when something goes wrong.

questions.q: How should the contractor decide the check-in times and the time limits for each escalation step?
o: Let each reader choose limits that suit her own day best
Copy the limits used for the staff in the company's office
Assess the risks and agree the limits before work starts
Set the limits after the first serious incident has occurred
questions.why: Time limits should come from a risk assessment and be agreed before work starts, so nobody has to guess when a missed check-in becomes an emergency.

questions.q: Ms Powell's Monday meeting runs two hours and she does most of the talking. Which change helps most?
o: Send an agenda, keep to time and ask each person to speak
Make attendance voluntary so that only interested officers join in
Replace the meeting with a long email sent each Monday morning
Move the meeting to 7:00 p.m. so that it can run as long as needed
questions.why: A prepared agenda, time-keeping and a round where everyone speaks make online meetings effective and inclusive. Voluntary attendance, a long email or an evening slot do not fix how the meeting is run.

questions.q: Devon often has a weak connection. How should Ms Powell help him take part?
o: Ask him to travel to the Kingston office for the meetings each week
Leave him out of the meeting and send him the notes afterwards
Offer a dial-in, summarise what he missed and ask for his views
Tell him to buy a better phone plan at his own cost
questions.why: The aim is to include him. A dial-in, a summary and another way to give his view keep him in the discussion. Exclusion or making him pay for a fix is unfair and loses his input.

questions.q: Shanice's report had many errors and she says she is worn out. What is the best way to give feedback?
o: In the Monday meeting so that others can learn from the same errors
Privately by call or video, with examples, and check her workload
By a sharp email that is copied to the director of the organisation
By waiting until her annual appraisal to mention the errors
questions.why: Private, specific feedback with a check on wellbeing and workload is fair and effective. Public criticism, copied emails and delay harm trust and ignore a possible stress problem.

questions.q: After the one-to-one with Shanice, what should Ms Powell do?
o: Say nothing more so that Shanice does not feel she is being watched closely
Post a note in the staff chat group so that everyone knows the plan
Wait for Shanice to raise the matter again if she needs more help
Send a short note of the actions agreed, with dates and a review time
questions.why: A written follow-up gives both people a clear record and shows commitment to the support agreed. It should be private, calm and clear, not shared with the whole team.

questions.q: Staff email files to each other and some use memory sticks. What should Mr Rose do?
o: Ask each person to delete emailed files from their own mailbox each evening
Provide secure shared storage and train staff on a written security policy
Let each person choose the method that they find fastest to use
Forbid all work on laptops outside the agency's office
questions.why: Staff need a secure, convenient alternative and clear rules. Deleting emails, free choice or banning offsite work do not control the risk or solve the problem.

questions.q: Staff sometimes work on public Wi-Fi in cafés. Which control best protects the agency's systems?
o: Use the company VPN, with strong passwords and two-step login
Avoid typing passwords while connected to a public network
Work only in the hours after the café has closed to the public
Ask clients to send their documents by post instead of online
questions.why: A VPN with strong authentication protects data on unsafe networks. The other options are unrealistic or leave the data exposed.

questions.q: A designer logs in at midnight to finish work. What should Mr Rose do?
o: Praise her publicly for her extra effort at the next team meeting
Ask her to send her emails only after midnight in future
Take no action unless the quality of her work falls
Check her workload and agree realistic deadlines and hours
questions.why: Late-night work can signal overload and risks burnout. A manager should check the workload and agree sustainable hours. Rewarding overwork encourages it.

questions.q: Mr Rose is thinking of software that records every screen all day. What should he consider first?
o: Whether competing agencies in Ocho Rios already use the same software
Whether the software costs less than holding weekly staff meetings
Whether it is necessary and proportionate, and whether staff are told
Whether staff are likely to notice that the software is running
questions.why: Monitoring must have a clear purpose, be proportionate and be disclosed, in line with the purpose of the data protection law. Clear targets and records are fairer and build more trust than secret monitoring.
